content.content:
1	# obsd
2	
3	Minimal, dependency-free backend skeleton for **metrics ingestion, alerting and
4	SLO tracking**. Python 3.10+, standard library only, offline, deterministic
5	(every time-dependent entry point takes an injected `now_ms`).
6	
7	The lane goal is a metrics collection, alerting and SLO backend that grows
8	towards time-series writes and downsampling, label indexing and a query subset,
9	aggregation and sliding windows, alert rules with silencing and inhibition,
10	notification routing and dedup, SLO and error-budget math, retention and
11	compaction, multi-tenant quota, access control and audit, and consistent reads
12	under high availability. This seed implements the first, smallest *real* slice of
13	each of those areas.
14	
15	## Run
16	
17	```bash
18	# HTTP API (data dir flag is global and comes BEFORE the subcommand)
19	python3 -m obsd --data-dir ./obsd_data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
20	
21	# test suite
22	python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
23	```
24	
25	Both commands are run offline with the system interpreter; no third-party
26	package is imported anywhere.
27	
28	## CLI
29	
30	`python3 -m obsd [--data-dir ./obsd_data] <command> ...` prints exactly one line
31	of JSON on stdout. On error it prints one line of JSON (`{"error":"..."}`) on
32	stderr and exits non-zero.
33	
34	| Command | Example |
35	| --- | --- |
36	| `serve` | `python3 -m obsd --data-dir ./obsd_data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080` |
37	| `quota-set` | `python3 -m obsd quota-set --tenant acme --max-series 1000 --max-points 1000000` |
38	| `quota-get` | `python3 -m obsd quota-get --tenant acme` |
39	| `write` | `python3 -m obsd write --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --label host=a --sample 1000:12.5 --now-ms 2000` |
40	| `write-batch` | `python3 -m obsd write-batch --entries '[{"tenant":"acme","metric":"latency_ms","samples":[[1000,12.5]]}]' --now-ms 2000` |
41	| `query` | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000 --step 1000 --agg avg` |
42	| `query` (grouped) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --agg avg --group-by '["host"]'` |
43	| `query` (matchers) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --matchers '[{"key":"host","op":"=~","value":"api-.*"}]'` |
44	| `query` (sliding window) | `python3 -m obsd query --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000 --step 1000 --window-ms 5000 --agg avg` |
45	| `export` | `python3 -m obsd export --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --start 0 --end 5000` |
46	| `replay` | `python3 -m obsd replay --snapshot '{"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[...]}' --now-ms 5000` |
47	| `rule-add` | `python3 -m obsd rule-add --tenant acme --metric latency_ms --comparator "<" --threshold 10 --window-ms 60000 --for-ms 30000 --agg avg --severity warning` |
48	| `eval` | `python3 -m obsd eval --now-ms 68000` |
49	| `alerts` | `python3 -m obsd alerts --tenant acme --state firing` |
50	| `silence-add` | `python3 -m obsd silence-add --tenant acme --starts-ms 0 --ends-ms 90000 --reason maintenance` |
51	| `route-add` | `python3 -m obsd route-add --tenant acme --target pager --label host=a --severity critical --event firing --repeat-ms 300000` |
52	| `route-list` | `python3 -m obsd route-list --tenant acme` |
53	| `notification-list` | `python3 -m obsd notification-list --tenant acme --acked false` |
54	| `notification-ack` | `python3 -m obsd notification-ack --id notification-00001` |
55	| `slo set` | `python3 -m obsd slo set --tenant acme --name availability --metric latency_ms --good-comparator ">=" --threshold 1 --target-ratio 0.9 --window-ms 60000` |
56	| `slo status` | `python3 -m obsd slo status --name availability --now-ms 60000` |
57	| `principal-create` | `python3 -m obsd principal-create --id ops --token s3cret --role admin --tenant acme --tenant globex` |
58	| `principal-list` | `python3 -m obsd principal-list` |
59	| `principal-revoke` | `python3 -m obsd principal-revoke --id ops` |
60	
61	## HTTP API
62	
63	Errors are always JSON: `{"error":"..."}` with status 400 (bad request),
64	404 (unknown resource) or 409 (write conflict or quota exceeded).
65	
66	| Method | Path | Request | Response |
67	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
68	| GET | `/healthz` | – | `200 {"ok":true}` |
69	| POST | `/v1/series` | `{"tenant","metric","labels","samples":[[ts,value],...]}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"series_id":"..."}`, `409` on conflicting timestamp or quota exceeded |
70	| POST | `/v1/series/batch` | `{"entries":[{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?},...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[{"series_id","written","duplicates"},...]}`, `400` on malformed entries, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
71	| GET | `/v1/query` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&step=&agg=&group_by=&window=&matchers=` (group_by and matchers are JSON arrays; matchers holds `{"key","op","value"}` objects) | `200 {"series":[{"labels":{...},"points":[[ts,value\|null],...]}]}` |
72	| GET | `/v1/export` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&matchers=` (same filters and closed-interval semantics as `/v1/query`) | `200 {"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[{"tenant","metric","labels","samples"},...]}` |
73	| POST | `/v1/replay` | `{"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?,"dry_run"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[...],"applied":true}` (`200` with `"applied":false` for a dry run), `400` on invalid input or digest mismatch, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
74	| POST | `/v1/quotas` | `{"tenant","max_series":n\|null,"max_points":n\|null}` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}`; invalid tenant/limits give `400` and leave config untouched |
75	| GET | `/v1/quotas` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` (unconfigured tenant reports `null` limits and real usage) |
76	| POST | `/v1/rules` | rule object | `201` stored rule |
77	| GET | `/v1/rules` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"rules":[...]}` |
78	| POST | `/v1/evaluate` | `{"now_ms":n}` | `200 {"firing":[...],"silenced":[...],"inhibited":[...],"resolved":[...]}` |
79	| GET | `/v1/alerts` | `?tenant=&state=` | `200 {"alerts":[...]}` |
80	| POST | `/v1/silences` | `{"tenant","labels","starts_ms","ends_ms","reason"}` | `201` stored silence |
81	| POST | `/v1/inhibitions` | `{"source_severity","target_severity","same_labels"}` | `201` stored inhibition |
82	| POST | `/v1/notification-routes` | `{"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?}` | `201` stored route; `400` invalid, `409` duplicate id |
83	| GET | `/v1/notification-routes` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"routes":[...]}` |
84	| DELETE | `/v1/notification-routes/{id}` | – | `200 {"deleted":id}`; `404` unknown route (notifications are kept) |
85	| GET | `/v1/notifications` | `?tenant=&route_id=&alert_id=&acked=` | `200 {"notifications":[...]}` (read-only, never consumes) |
86	| POST | `/v1/notifications/{id}/ack` | – | `200` stored notification (re-ack returns the same record); `404` unknown notification |
87	| POST | `/v1/slos` | `{"tenant","name","metric","labels","good_comparator","threshold","target_ratio","window_ms"}` | `201` stored SLO |
88	| GET | `/v1/slos/status` | `?tenant=&name=&now_ms=` | `200` SLO status object |
89	| GET | `/v1/stats` | – | `200 {"store":{...},"alerts":n}` |
90	| GET | `/v1/audit` | `?tenant=&principal_id=&outcome=&after_seq=&limit=` | `200 {"entries":[{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"},...]}` ascending by `seq` (admin only) |
91	
92	**Access control and audit.** Principals are managed locally through the CLI
93	(`principal-create`/`principal-list`/`principal-revoke`); a principal is a
94	unique `--id`, a non-empty `--token`, a `--role` of `viewer`, `writer` or
95	`admin`, and at least one `--tenant` scope. Only the token's SHA-256 digest is
96	persisted (`access.json`); the token itself never appears in any output,
97	listing or audit record. A duplicate id is a conflict (`409` semantics), an
98	unknown id on revoke is `unknown principal: ...` (`404` semantics). While no
99	`access.json` exists, access control is off: every request stays anonymous,
100	nothing returns `401`/`403`, no audit records are written and `/healthz` is
101	always public either way.
102	
103	Once the config exists, every non-`/healthz` request must carry
104	`Authorization: Bearer <token>`: a missing, malformed or unknown token gets
105	`401 {"error":"unauthorized"}`. An authenticated principal whose role or
106	tenant scope does not cover the request gets `403 {"error":"forbidden"}`.
107	`viewer` reads resources inside its tenant scope; `writer` additionally
108	writes series, manages rules, silences, routes and SLOs and acknowledges
109	notifications inside its scope; `admin` additionally runs quotas, inhibitions,
110	evaluation, stats and the audit endpoint, and is the only role allowed to run
111	cross-tenant operations (requests with no single tenant, such as an
112	unfiltered `GET /v1/alerts`). Batch writes are checked per entry: if any
113	entry's tenant is outside the caller's scope the whole batch is rejected with
114	`403` before anything is written, preserving atomicity. Principals created or
115	revoked through the CLI take effect on a running server without a restart.
116	
117	Every non-`/healthz` request — authentication rejections, authorization
118	denials and business failures included — appends one persistent audit record
119	to `audit.jsonl` with a monotonically increasing `seq`:
120	`{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"}`, where
121	`principal_id` is `null` when the request could not be authenticated,
122	`tenant` is `null` when the request has no single tenant, and `outcome` is
123	`allowed` (authorized, status < 400), `denied` (`401`/`403`) or `failed`
124	(authorized but the business logic rejected it). The log is reloaded on
125	startup, so records and the `seq` sequence survive restarts.
126	`GET /v1/audit` (admin only) filters by `tenant`, `principal_id`, `outcome`
127	and `after_seq` (entries with `seq > after_seq`) and pages with a positive
128	integer `limit`; invalid filters are `400`, non-admin access is `403`.
129	
130	## Data model
131	
132	A series identity is `(tenant, metric, sorted(label pairs))`. The canonical
133	identity string joins the tenant, the metric and every `key=value` label pair
134	(sorted by key) with `\n`:
135	
136	```
137	acme\nlatency_ms\nhost=a\nregion=eu
138	```
139	
140	`series_id = sha256(canonical_identity).hexdigest()`, so the same logical series
141	always maps to the same 64-character id, independent of label insertion order.
142	
143	Storage layout (all writes atomic via temp file + `os.replace`):
144	
145	```
146	<data-dir>/series.json              registry: series_id -> tenant/metric/labels
147	<data-dir>/points/<series_id>.jsonl one {"t":ts,"v":value} object per line
148	<data-dir>/quotas.json              tenant -> {"max_series","max_points"} limits
149	<data-dir>/rules.json               <data-dir>/alerts.json
150	<data-dir>/slos.json                <data-dir>/silences.json
151	<data-dir>/inhibitions.json         <data-dir>/counters.json
152	<data-dir>/routes.json              <data-dir>/notifications.json
153	<data-dir>/notify_state.json        per-(route, alert) notification dedup state
154	<data-dir>/access.json              principals: id, token SHA-256 digest, role, tenants
155	<data-dir>/audit.jsonl              one audit record per line, seq monotonically increasing
156	```
157	
158	A directory written before quotas existed simply has no `quotas.json`, which
159	means every tenant is unlimited; limits and usage are reloaded together on
160	construction so a reopen always reports a consistent snapshot.
161	
162	`SeriesStore` and `AlertEngine` each guard their state with a
163	`threading.RLock`, so the threaded HTTP server can serve concurrent requests; all
164	state is reloaded from disk on construction, so a restart preserves series,
165	points, rules, alerts, silences, inhibitions, SLOs, notification routes and
166	queued notifications.
167	
168	## Semantics and formulas
169	
170	**Idempotent write.** `write(tenant, metric, labels, samples, now=None,
171	overwrite=False)` stores `(timestamp_ms, value)` pairs. Writing an existing
172	`(series, timestamp)` with the *same* value is a duplicate: it changes nothing
173	and is counted in `duplicates`. A *different* value for a stored timestamp is a
174	conflict: it raises `ObsError` (`409` over HTTP) unless `overwrite=True`, in
175	which case the stored value is replaced and counted in `written`. A timestamp
176	greater than the injected `now` (when `now` is given) is rejected.
177	
178	**Atomic multi-series write.** `write_batch(entries, now=None, overwrite=False)`
179	(also `POST /v1/series/batch` and the CLI `write-batch --entries '<json>'`)
180	applies a non-empty list of `{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?}` entries
181	(`labels` omitted means `{}`, no other keys allowed) as one all-or-nothing
182	unit. Entries may span tenants and metrics and may repeat a series. `now` is
183	`null`/omitted (no future check) or a non-boolean integer; `overwrite` must be
184	a boolean (default `false`). The whole batch is validated before any conflict
185	is reported, and all conflicts before any quota check. Entries and their
186	samples are then applied in input order, so a later entry sees the earlier
187	entries of the same batch: a same-value restatement is a duplicate, a
188	differing value conflicts unless `overwrite` (then it replaces and counts as
189	written). The result is `{"written","duplicates","results"}` with one
190	`{"series_id","written","duplicates"}` per entry in input order; the totals
191	are the per-entry sums. A successful batch with `written > 0` increases
192	`stats()["writes"]` by exactly one; a pure-duplicate batch increases nothing.
193	Quotas are charged per tenant with the batch's net new series and distinct new
194	timestamps — duplicates and overwrites add no occupancy, and only dimensions
195	that actually increase are checked. Any rejection (structure, missing fields,
196	per-entry validation, future samples → `400`; conflict or quota → `409`)
197	leaves no series, sample or write-count change behind, on disk included, and
198	concurrent queries and quota reads only ever see the state before or after the
199	whole batch. Replaying the same batch re-judges duplicates and overwrites in
200	the same order.
201	
202	**Snapshot export and replay.** `export_snapshot(tenant, metric, labels=None,
203	start_ms=None, end_ms=None, matchers=None)` (also `GET /v1/export` and the CLI
204	`export`) captures the raw samples of every matching series as a verifiable
205	document `{"version": 1, "snapshot_id": ..., "entries": [...]}`. The filters
206	and the closed `[start_ms, end_ms]` interval behave exactly as in `query`.
207	Each entry holds only `tenant`, `metric`, `labels` and `samples` (ascending by
208	timestamp); entries are ordered by `series_id` and registered series with no
209	sample in range are omitted. `snapshot_id` is the SHA-256 of the sorted,
210	compact JSON UTF-8 bytes of `{"version": 1, "entries": [...]}`. The export
211	reads one coherent snapshot under a single lock acquisition and never changes
212	write counters, quotas, alerts or query results, so exporting the same state
213	twice yields identical content.
214	
215	`replay_snapshot(snapshot, now_ms=None, overwrite=False, dry_run=False)` (also
216	`POST /v1/replay` and the CLI `replay --snapshot '<json>'`) verifies the
217	document before storing anything: the version must be 1, `snapshot_id` must
218	match the entries digest, and every entry then goes through the `write_batch`
219	rules (labels, samples, future timestamps against `now_ms` when given,
220	conflicts, per-tenant quotas). Invalid input or a digest mismatch is a `400`,
221	a conflict or quota breach a `409`, and any failure leaves no in-memory or
222	on-disk change behind. The result is `{"written", "duplicates", "results",
223	"applied"}` with `results` in entry order. A dry run (`dry_run=true` /
224	`--dry-run`) performs all validation and counting but applies nothing and
225	reports `applied: false`; a real replay reports `applied: true` (`202` over
226	HTTP, `200` for a dry run). Replaying a snapshot onto the state it came from
227	is a pure duplicate replay (`written == 0`, the write counter does not move),
228	replaying onto a partial state fills in only the missing points, and a replay
229	after a restart re-judges exactly as an in-process one. Replay never mints new
230	series identities and does not alter labels, tenant isolation, query
231	aggregation, alert or SLO semantics. With access control enabled, export is a
232	`read` operation scoped to the requested tenant and replay is a `write`
233	operation checked per entry — any entry outside the caller's scope rejects the
234	whole replay with `403` — and both are audited like every other endpoint.
235	
236	**Bucketing.** `query(..., step_ms=step, agg=agg)` assigns a sample with
237	timestamp `t` to bucket `b = t - (t % step)`, i.e. buckets are
238	left-closed/right-open (`[b, b+step)`) on epoch multiples. Every bucket from the
239	first non-empty bucket to the last non-empty bucket that also lies inside
240	`[start_ms, end_ms]` is emitted, and buckets with no sample are emitted as
241	`[b, null]`. Bucket value = `agg` over the samples in the bucket, where `agg` is
242	one of `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`. A series whose range contains no
243	sample is still listed with an empty `points` list. With `agg` and *no*
244	`step_ms` the whole `[start_ms, end_ms]` range is a single bucket. With neither,
245	raw samples are returned in `[timestamp, value]` order. `rollup(tenant, metric,
246	labels, window_ms, agg)` is `query` with `step_ms = window_ms` over the whole
247	stored range, with empty buckets dropped; output is ordered by `series_id`, so
248	it is deterministic.
249	
250	**Label matchers.** In addition to exact `labels` / `label.k=v` filtering,
251	`query` accepts `matchers` (`matchers` on `GET /v1/query`, `--matchers` on the
252	CLI): a JSON array of objects containing exactly `key` (non-empty string),
253	`op` and `value` (string, may be empty). Ops are `=` / `!=` (exact whole-string
254	equality and negation) and `=~` / `!~` (Python `re` syntax matched against the
255	*whole* label value via full match, case-sensitive and Unicode-aware, and its
256	negation). Omitting the parameter, passing Python `None`, or sending `[]` adds
257	no condition; an explicit JSON `null` or empty text is rejected (HTTP/CLI).
258	Matchers combine with each other and with the exact label filters by logical
259	AND — including several matchers on the same key — apply to raw series labels
260	before bucketing or grouping (labels absent from `group_by` count too), and are
261	restricted to the requested `tenant` and `metric`; `tenant`, `metric` and
262	`series_id` are not implicit labels. A missing key never satisfies `=`/`=~` but
263	always satisfies `!=`/`!~`, so `=~ ""` selects only series where the key exists
264	with an empty value (grouping still separates a missing key from an empty
265	value). `api-.*` matches `api-a` but not `xapi-a`. Duplicate matchers never
266	duplicate series, matcher order is irrelevant, and contradictory matchers
267	yield an empty result. Invalid JSON, a non-array, non-object elements, missing
268	or extra fields, wrong types, an empty `key`, an unsupported `op` or an invalid
269	regex raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON error line on stderr for the
270	CLI); every matcher is validated even when no candidate series exists.
271	
272	**Grouped query.** `query(..., agg=agg, group_by=[keys...])` aggregates *across*
273	series: matching series (same tenant/metric/label filters and `[start_ms,
274	end_ms]` range as above) are bucketed into groups by the values of the given
275	label keys, and the raw in-range samples of all series in a group are pooled
276	before `agg` is applied — samples from different series at the same timestamp
277	count individually. `group_by=[]` merges every matching series into one group.
278	Each result row carries only `labels` (the group keys actually present on the
279	group's series — a missing key and an empty-string value form different
280	groups) and `points`; rows are ordered lexicographically by their sorted label
281	pairs. Bucketing follows the same rules as the per-series query (epoch-aligned
282	left-closed buckets with `null` gaps, or a single point at the group's
283	earliest sample without `step_ms`). A group whose series have no sample in
284	range is still listed with empty `points`; no matching series at all yields an
285	empty `series` array. `group_by` must be a list of distinct non-empty strings
286	and requires `agg`; violations raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON
287	error line on stderr for the CLI).
288	
289	**Sliding-window query.** `query(..., start_ms=start, end_ms=end, step_ms=step,
290	agg=agg, window_ms=window)` switches to a separate mode the moment `window_ms`
291	is supplied (it is optional in every binding: `window` on `GET /v1/query`,
292	`--window-ms` on the CLI). In this mode `start_ms`, `end_ms`, `step_ms` and
293	`agg` are all required; `start_ms` and `end_ms` must be integer milliseconds,
294	`step_ms` and `window_ms` positive integer milliseconds, and `end_ms >=
295	start_ms` (bools, fractions and missing/unknown values are rejected). Evaluation
296	times are `t = start + k*step` for `k = 0, 1, ...`, keeping only times
297	`t <= end`; the output point timestamp is the evaluation time itself. The step
298	need not divide the window and windows are never aligned to fixed buckets.
299	
300	Each evaluation aggregates the raw samples in the half-open interval
301	`(t - window_ms, t]`: the left edge is excluded (a sample exactly one window
302	length earlier does not count), the right edge included (a sample at `t`
303	does). `start_ms` only constrains the output grid — the first window at
304	`start` also reads history older than `start`; no window ever reads a sample
305	newer than its own evaluation time. The aggregation uses the same meanings as
306	bucketing (`sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`), and a window containing no
307	sample emits `[t, null]` for *every* aggregation, including `count`.
308	
309	Every matching registered series is returned on the full time grid even when
310	all of its windows are empty; no matching series yields an empty `series`
311	array. The Python per-series rows keep `series_id`; HTTP and CLI keep the
312	existing result shape. With `group_by`, all raw samples of the group's series
313	that fall in each window are pooled before aggregating (samples sharing a
314	timestamp across series count individually, `avg` divides by the total sample
315	count), a missing group key and an empty-string value stay distinct groups,
316	and each group keeps the full grid, fully null when no sample ever falls in a
317	window. Group filtering, ordering and validation follow the ordinary grouped
318	rules. The whole query reads one coherent snapshot, so concurrent writes or
319	retention sweeps can never mix old and new data; queries never alter samples,
320	counters or configuration, and the same history gives identical results after
321	reopening the store. Omitting `window_ms` preserves the previous query
322	behaviour exactly — `rollup`, write idempotency/overwrite, quotas, alerts and
323	SLOs are unaffected.
324	
325	**Counter aggregates.** In sliding-window mode `agg` also accepts `increase`
326	and `rate` (query entries only — `rollup`, alert rules and SLOs still reject
327	them, and using them without `window_ms` fails the query). Each matching
328	series is treated as a counter: within `(t - window_ms, t]` the time-sorted
329	adjacent readings contribute their difference when non-decreasing, while a
330	drop is a counter reset contributing only the later reading; the first reading
331	contributes nothing. Only samples actually inside the window are used — no
332	boundary borrowing, interpolation or extrapolation by window length.
333	`increase` is the sum of those deltas, `rate` that sum divided by the seconds
334	between the window's first and last sample. A window with fewer than two
335	distinct sample timestamps emits `[t, null]`; unchanged readings emit `0`.
336	Grouped queries compute each series independently and sum the non-null
337	per-series results (never differencing across series); a group whose series
338	are all null at a time emits null there. Any matched sample that actually
339	falls into an output window and is negative or non-finite fails the whole
340	query (`ObsError`, HTTP `400`, CLI non-zero with a one-line JSON error);
341	samples outside every window or filtered out by labels/matchers are never
342	inspected, and parameters are validated even when no series matches.
343	
344	**Retention.** `enforce_retention(tenant, cutoff_ms)` removes every sample of
345	that tenant with `timestamp_millis < cutoff_ms` and rewrites the affected point
346	files. `stats()` returns `{"series","points","writes","tenants"}`.
347	
348	**Per-tenant quotas.** `set_quota(tenant, max_series, max_points)` sets the
349	tenant-wide limits; each limit is a non-negative integer or `null` (omitted
350	fields over HTTP also mean `null`, i.e. unlimited), and `0` forbids adding any.
351	`get_quota(tenant)` returns
352	`{"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` — the configured
353	limits and the current usage in one snapshot. Configuring a quota never creates
354	a series, and an unconfigured tenant is unlimited. Limits apply to all of a
355	tenant's metrics together: `series` is the number of registered series and
356	`points` the total number of *distinct timestamps* across those series, not
357	physical point-file lines. Label order, same-value replays, overwritten points
358	and a timestamp repeated inside one batch add no occupancy.
359	
360	Every write path (`SeriesStore.write`/`write_batch`, `POST /v1/series` and
361	`/v1/series/batch`, the CLI `write`/`write-batch`) is
362	checked after the existing input validation and conflict rules, using the
363	batch's net increase: a batch is rejected (ObsError / HTTP `409` / CLI JSON
364	error with non-zero exit) when *either* dimension it increases would exceed its
365	limit, and the rejection leaves no new series, samples or write-count change.
366	Limits may be lowered below current usage; afterwards only the dimensions a
367	write actually increases are checked — an already-over-limit dimension blocks
368	nothing by itself, so pure duplicates and overwrites keep succeeding. Retention
369	frees the occupancy of deleted points, while empty series stay registered.
370	Overwrites rewrite the point file so one timestamp never occupies two lines; on
371	reopen, any duplicate timestamp lines (including those left by older builds)
372	collapse to the last value, so historical re-overwrites never double-count.
373	
374	**Rule shape.** `{"id","tenant","metric","labels","comparator" ∈ {">",">=","<",
375	"<=","==","!="},"threshold","for_ms","window_ms","agg","severity" ∈ {"info",
376	"warning","critical"},"annotations"}`. `add_rule` validates every field and
377	raises `ObsError` for anything malformed (`id` is generated when omitted).
378	
379	**Evaluation window.** Let `step = window_ms`, `t = now_ms` and
380	`bucket_start(t) = t - (t % step)`. The window is
381	`[bucket_start(t) - step, t]`, i.e. the current bucket plus the whole previous
382	bucket. The rule condition holds for a series when *every* non-empty bucket in
383	that window satisfies `comparator(value, threshold)` — one violating bucket
384	anywhere in the window stops the condition, and it keeps stopping it until that
385	bucket has left the window.
386	
387	**`for_ms`.** Let `run_start` be the timestamp of the first bucket of the
388	current unbroken run of satisfying buckets (a violating bucket resets the run).
389	The rule fires only when the condition holds *and*
390	`bucket_start(now_ms) - run_start >= for_ms`. With `for_ms = 0`, one satisfied
391	bucket is enough; with `for_ms = window_ms`, the current and the previous bucket
392	must both be satisfied. Before the hold time is reached the alert is recorded
393	with `firing = false` and appears in none of the four output lists.
394	
395	**Alert identity and dedup.** Alert identity is `(rule_id, series_id)`, distinct
396	from the alert id. The first time a condition holds an alert id
397	`alert-NNNNN` is minted for that identity and reused forever: re-evaluating an
398	unchanged condition returns the *same* `id` and increments `occurrences` (the
399	number of evaluations in which the condition held). `since_ms` is `run_start`,
400	not the evaluation time, so dedup does not depend on the wall clock.
401	
402	**Resolution.** When the condition stops holding, the alert's state becomes
403	`resolved`, `firing` becomes `false`, `resolved_ms` is set once, and the alert is
404	reported in the `resolved` list of that evaluation. If the same condition holds
405	again later, the *same alert id* is reused and `occurrences` keeps counting.
406	Because the condition covers the whole window, a series that produced one bad
407	bucket stays unresolved until that bucket has left the window.
408	
409	**Silence vs inhibition precedence.** A condition that holds and whose `for_ms`
410	is satisfied is first checked against active silences: a silence is active when
411	`starts_ms <= now_ms <= ends_ms`, the tenant matches and every silence label
412	matcher is present in the series labels. Inside an active silence the alert state
413	is `silenced` (it is *not* firing) and the silence id and reason are recorded.
414	Only if no silence matches is inhibition checked: an inhibition
415	`(source_severity, target_severity, same_labels)` marks a `target_severity` alert
416	as `inhibited` while an alert of at least `source_severity` is currently
417	`firing` in the same tenant with *exactly the same label set*. Silence therefore
418	wins over inhibition. A silenced or inhibited alert still counts its
419	`occurrences` and returns to `firing` as soon as the silence/inhibition no longer
420	applies. `list_alerts(state=None)` filters by `firing`, `silenced`, `inhibited`
421	or `resolved`.
422	
423	**Notification routing.** `add_route({"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,
424	"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?})` registers a notification route; `tenant` and
425	`target` are required non-empty strings, `labels` is an exact label subset the
426	alert's series must contain, `severities` (default: all severities) and
427	`events` (default: `["firing","resolved"]`, the only two allowed values) are
428	non-empty arrays when given, and `repeat_ms` is `null` or a non-negative
429	integer. Invalid shapes raise `ObsError` (HTTP `400`), a duplicate `id` is a
430	conflict (HTTP `409`), an unknown route is `404`; without an `id` the route is
431	named `route-NNNN`. Deleting a route keeps its historical notifications.
432	
433	`evaluate(now_ms)` still returns only the four state lists, but every alert
434	transition also appends to the notification queue of each matching route
435	(tenant equal, route labels a subset of the series labels, alert severity in
436	`severities`): an alert that enters `firing` — the first time, or when
437	recovering from `silenced`/`inhibited` — produces one `firing` record; while
438	the same firing state continues a repeat is emitted only when `repeat_ms` is
439	set and that much time has passed since the route's last notification for the
440	alert; entering `resolved` produces exactly one `resolved` record. Pending
441	(`for_ms` not yet met), silenced and inhibited alerts never produce `firing`
442	records. Dedup is tracked per route, so routes notify independently. Each
443	record is `{"id": "notification-NNNNN","route_id","alert_id","tenant",
444	"target","event","created_ms","alert": <snapshot>,"acked": false}` and is
445	persisted across restarts together with the dedup state.
446	`list_notifications(tenant, route_id, alert_id, acked)` reads the queue
447	without consuming it; `ack_notification(id)` marks a record acknowledged,
448	returns the same record on a repeated ack and raises `ObsError` (HTTP `404`)
449	for an unknown id.
450	
451	**SLO and error budget.** `set_slo(tenant, name, metric, labels,
452	good_comparator, threshold, target_ratio, window_ms)` defines a good-events
453	ratio SLO. `slo_status(name, now_ms, tenant=None)` counts every stored sample of
454	the matching series inside `[now_ms - window_ms, now_ms]`:
455	
456	```
457	total          = number of samples in the window (nulls excluded)
458	good           = samples where compare(value, good_comparator, threshold)
459	bad            = total - good
460	ratio          = good / total                             (0.0 when total == 0)
461	error_budget   = max(0.0, 1 - (1 - ratio) / (1 - target_ratio))   (target_ratio < 1)
462	               = 1.0 if ratio >= 1.0 else 0.0              (target_ratio == 1)
463	burn_rate      = (bad / total) / (1 - target_ratio)        (0.0 when target_ratio >= 1 or total == 0)
464	met            = ratio >= target_ratio
465	```
466	
467	`ratio` is the observed good ratio, `target_ratio ∈ (0,1]` the objective,
468	`burn_rate` how fast the budget is being spent relative to the allowed bad rate
469	(`1.0` means exactly on budget, `> 1.0` means burning too fast) and
470	`error_budget` the *fraction of the allowed error budget still unspent*:
471	`1.0` means untouched, `0.0` means exhausted or exceeded. For any `ratio` that
472	meets the target the two written forms of `error_budget` are identical, since
473	`1 - (1-ratio)/(1-target) = (ratio - target)/(1 - target)` and
474	`1 - ratio/target = (target - ratio)/target` are both non-negative only inside
475	their own regime; the first form is the one used, because it degrades sensibly
476	when the ratio beats the target (more budget left) instead of pinning to `0`.
477	With `total == 0` the ratio is `0.0`, so the budget counts as exhausted.
478	
479	Examples: 9 good + 1 bad with `target_ratio = 0.9` gives `ratio = 0.9`,
480	`error_budget = 0.0`, `burn_rate = 0.1/0.1 = 1.0`, `met = true` (exactly on
481	budget). 98 good + 2 bad with `target_ratio = 0.95` gives `ratio = 0.98`,
482	`burn_rate = 0.02/0.05 = 0.4` and `error_budget = 1 - 0.02/0.05 = 0.6` (60% of
483	the budget still unspent). 90 good + 10 bad with `target_ratio = 0.99` gives
484	`ratio = 0.9`, `burn_rate = 10.0`, `error_budget = 0.0`, `met = false`.
485	
486	**Determinism.** No module calls `time.time()` inside decision logic: `now_ms` is
487	passed into `evaluate`, `slo_status` and `write` (the HTTP layer uses the wall
488	clock only when a caller omits `now_ms` on `GET /v1/slos/status`, and
489	`/v1/slos/status` requires it in the CLI).
490	
491	## Layout
492	
493	```
494	obsd/__init__.py    public exports
495	obsd/tsdb.py        SeriesStore
496	obsd/alerts.py      AlertEngine
497	obsd/access.py      AccessControl (principals + audit log)
498	obsd/http_app.py    ThreadingHTTPServer + create_server
499	obsd/cli.py         command line interface
500	obsd/__main__.py    python3 -m obsd entry point
501	tests/              unittest suite (tsdb, alerts, http, access)
502	```
503	
504	## Tests
505	
506	```bash
507	python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
508	```
509	
510	Covered: series identity and label-order independence, idempotent re-write,
511	conflicting-timestamp rejection and `overwrite`, range filtering, epoch-aligned
512	buckets, null buckets, all five aggregations, deterministic rollups,
513	sliding-window grids with left-open/right-closed windows, null empty windows
514	(including count), full grids for empty series and groups, window argument
515	validation across Python/HTTP/CLI, window snapshot consistency under
516	concurrent writes and retention, retention,
517	restart safety, rule validation, `for_ms` timing, dedup with occurrence
518	counting, resolution and re-firing (including the window that keeps a bad bucket
519	blocking), silence scoping and expiry, inhibition by severity and exact label
520	set, SLO/error-budget/burn-rate math (including the empty window), quota
521	configuration/validation, net-increase enforcement and whole-batch rejection,
522	zero/lowered limits with duplicates and overwrites, tenant isolation, quota
523	release under retention, quota/usage consistency after reopen (including
524	collapsed duplicate timestamp lines), concurrent writes/reconfiguration/pruning,
525	atomic multi-series batches (cross-tenant/cross-metric entries, in-batch
526	duplicate/overwrite ordering, all-or-nothing rejection on disk, per-tenant net
527	quota accounting, single write-count increment, and the HTTP/CLI surfaces),
528	principal create/list/revoke with digest-only token persistence, role and
529	tenant-scope enforcement (`401`/`403`) with the anonymous surface unchanged
530	while access control is off, per-entry batch authorization with atomic
531	rejection, the persistent audit log (seq monotonic across restarts, filters
532	and `limit` pagination on `GET /v1/audit`),
533	verifiable snapshot export (filters, ordering, digest, side-effect-free
534	repeatability across restarts) and replay (roundtrip migration, duplicate and
535	missing-point re-judgement, dry runs, digest/validation/conflict/quota
536	rejection without a trace, per-entry authorization, and the HTTP/CLI
537	surfaces),
538	and the live HTTP surface over a real socket.
539	
540	Everything is deterministic: the suite injects every timestamp it uses, and the
541	modules never read the wall clock inside decision logic.
542

file.content:
# obsd

Minimal, dependency-free backend skeleton for **metrics ingestion, alerting and
SLO tracking**. Python 3.10+, standard library only, offline, deterministic
(every time-dependent entry point takes an injected `now_ms`).

The lane goal is a metrics collection, alerting and SLO backend that grows
towards time-series writes and downsampling, label indexing and a query subset,
aggregation and sliding windows, alert rules with silencing and inhibition,
notification routing and dedup, SLO and error-budget math, retention and
compaction, multi-tenant quota, access control and audit, and consistent reads
under high availability. This seed implements the first, smallest *real* slice of
each of those areas.

## Run

```bash
# HTTP API (data dir flag is global and comes BEFORE the subcommand)
python3 -m obsd --data-dir ./obsd_data serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080

# test suite
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Both commands are run offline with the system interpreter; no third-party
package is imported anywhere.

## HTTP API

Errors are always JSON: `{"error":"..."}` with status 400 (bad request),
404 (unknown resource) or 409 (write conflict or quota exceeded).

| Method | Path | Request | Response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/healthz` | – | `200 {"ok":true}` |
| POST | `/v1/series` | `{"tenant","metric","labels","samples":[[ts,value],...]}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"series_id":"..."}`, `409` on conflicting timestamp or quota exceeded |
| POST | `/v1/series/batch` | `{"entries":[{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?},...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[{"series_id","written","duplicates"},...]}`, `400` on malformed entries, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
| GET | `/v1/query` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&step=&agg=&group_by=&window=&matchers=` (group_by and matchers are JSON arrays; matchers holds `{"key","op","value"}` objects) | `200 {"series":[{"labels":{...},"points":[[ts,value\|null],...]}]}` |
| GET | `/v1/export` | `?tenant=&metric=&label.k=v&start=&end=&matchers=` (same filters and closed-interval semantics as `/v1/query`) | `200 {"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[{"tenant","metric","labels","samples"},...]}` |
| POST | `/v1/replay` | `{"version":1,"snapshot_id":"...","entries":[...],"now_ms"?,"overwrite"?,"dry_run"?}` | `202 {"written":n,"duplicates":m,"results":[...],"applied":true}` (`200` with `"applied":false` for a dry run), `400` on invalid input or digest mismatch, `409` on conflict or quota exceeded |
| POST | `/v1/quotas` | `{"tenant","max_series":n\|null,"max_points":n\|null}` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}`; invalid tenant/limits give `400` and leave config untouched |
| GET | `/v1/quotas` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` (unconfigured tenant reports `null` limits and real usage) |
| POST | `/v1/rules` | rule object | `201` stored rule |
| GET | `/v1/rules` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"rules":[...]}` |
| POST | `/v1/evaluate` | `{"now_ms":n}` | `200 {"firing":[...],"silenced":[...],"inhibited":[...],"resolved":[...]}` |
| GET | `/v1/alerts` | `?tenant=&state=` | `200 {"alerts":[...]}` |
| POST | `/v1/silences` | `{"tenant","labels","starts_ms","ends_ms","reason"}` | `201` stored silence |
| POST | `/v1/inhibitions` | `{"source_severity","target_severity","same_labels"}` | `201` stored inhibition |
| POST | `/v1/notification-routes` | `{"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?}` | `201` stored route; `400` invalid, `409` duplicate id |
| GET | `/v1/notification-routes` | `?tenant=` | `200 {"routes":[...]}` |
| DELETE | `/v1/notification-routes/{id}` | – | `200 {"deleted":id}`; `404` unknown route (notifications are kept) |
| GET | `/v1/notifications` | `?tenant=&route_id=&alert_id=&acked=` | `200 {"notifications":[...]}` (read-only, never consumes) |
| POST | `/v1/notifications/{id}/ack` | – | `200` stored notification (re-ack returns the same record); `404` unknown notification |
| POST | `/v1/slos` | `{"tenant","name","metric","labels","good_comparator","threshold","target_ratio","window_ms"}` | `201` stored SLO |
| GET | `/v1/slos/status` | `?tenant=&name=&now_ms=` | `200` SLO status object |
| GET | `/v1/stats` | – | `200 {"store":{...},"alerts":n}` |
| GET | `/v1/audit` | `?tenant=&principal_id=&outcome=&after_seq=&limit=` | `200 {"entries":[{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"},...]}` ascending by `seq` (admin only) |

**Access control and audit.** Principals are managed locally through the CLI
(`principal-create`/`principal-list`/`principal-revoke`); a principal is a
unique `--id`, a non-empty `--token`, a `--role` of `viewer`, `writer` or
`admin`, and at least one `--tenant` scope. Only the token's SHA-256 digest is
persisted (`access.json`); the token itself never appears in any output,
listing or audit record. A duplicate id is a conflict (`409` semantics), an
unknown id on revoke is `unknown principal: ...` (`404` semantics). While no
`access.json` exists, access control is off: every request stays anonymous,
nothing returns `401`/`403`, no audit records are written and `/healthz` is
always public either way.

Once the config exists, every non-`/healthz` request must carry
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`: a missing, malformed or unknown token gets
`401 {"error":"unauthorized"}`. An authenticated principal whose role or
tenant scope does not cover the request gets `403 {"error":"forbidden"}`.
`viewer` reads resources inside its tenant scope; `writer` additionally
writes series, manages rules, silences, routes and SLOs and acknowledges
notifications inside its scope; `admin` additionally runs quotas, inhibitions,
evaluation, stats and the audit endpoint, and is the only role allowed to run
cross-tenant operations (requests with no single tenant, such as an
unfiltered `GET /v1/alerts`). Batch writes are checked per entry: if any
entry's tenant is outside the caller's scope the whole batch is rejected with
`403` before anything is written, preserving atomicity. Principals created or
revoked through the CLI take effect on a running server without a restart.

Every non-`/healthz` request — authentication rejections, authorization
denials and business failures included — appends one persistent audit record
to `audit.jsonl` with a monotonically increasing `seq`:
`{"seq","principal_id","method","path","tenant","outcome","status"}`, where
`principal_id` is `null` when the request could not be authenticated,
`tenant` is `null` when the request has no single tenant, and `outcome` is
`allowed` (authorized, status < 400), `denied` (`401`/`403`) or `failed`
(authorized but the business logic rejected it). The log is reloaded on
startup, so records and the `seq` sequence survive restarts.
`GET /v1/audit` (admin only) filters by `tenant`, `principal_id`, `outcome`
and `after_seq` (entries with `seq > after_seq`) and pages with a positive
integer `limit`; invalid filters are `400`, non-admin access is `403`.

## Data model

A series identity is `(tenant, metric, sorted(label pairs))`. The canonical
identity string joins the tenant, the metric and every `key=value` label pair
(sorted by key) with `\n`:

```
acme\nlatency_ms\nhost=a\nregion=eu
```

`series_id = sha256(canonical_identity).hexdigest()`, so the same logical series
always maps to the same 64-character id, independent of label insertion order.

Storage layout (all writes atomic via temp file + `os.replace`):

```
<data-dir>/series.json              registry: series_id -> tenant/metric/labels
<data-dir>/points/<series_id>.jsonl one {"t":ts,"v":value} object per line
<data-dir>/quotas.json              tenant -> {"max_series","max_points"} limits
<data-dir>/rules.json               <data-dir>/alerts.json
<data-dir>/slos.json                <data-dir>/silences.json
<data-dir>/inhibitions.json         <data-dir>/counters.json
<data-dir>/routes.json              <data-dir>/notifications.json
<data-dir>/notify_state.json        per-(route, alert) notification dedup state
<data-dir>/access.json              principals: id, token SHA-256 digest, role, tenants
<data-dir>/audit.jsonl              one audit record per line, seq monotonically increasing
```

A directory written before quotas existed simply has no `quotas.json`, which
means every tenant is unlimited; limits and usage are reloaded together on
construction so a reopen always reports a consistent snapshot.

`SeriesStore` and `AlertEngine` each guard their state with a
`threading.RLock`, so the threaded HTTP server can serve concurrent requests; all
state is reloaded from disk on construction, so a restart preserves series,
points, rules, alerts, silences, inhibitions, SLOs, notification routes and
queued notifications.

## Semantics and formulas

**Idempotent write.** `write(tenant, metric, labels, samples, now=None,
overwrite=False)` stores `(timestamp_ms, value)` pairs. Writing an existing
`(series, timestamp)` with the *same* value is a duplicate: it changes nothing
and is counted in `duplicates`. A *different* value for a stored timestamp is a
conflict: it raises `ObsError` (`409` over HTTP) unless `overwrite=True`, in
which case the stored value is replaced and counted in `written`. A timestamp
greater than the injected `now` (when `now` is given) is rejected.

**Atomic multi-series write.** `write_batch(entries, now=None, overwrite=False)`
(also `POST /v1/series/batch` and the CLI `write-batch --entries '<json>'`)
applies a non-empty list of `{"tenant","metric","samples","labels"?}` entries
(`labels` omitted means `{}`, no other keys allowed) as one all-or-nothing
unit. Entries may span tenants and metrics and may repeat a series. `now` is
`null`/omitted (no future check) or a non-boolean integer; `overwrite` must be
a boolean (default `false`). The whole batch is validated before any conflict
is reported, and all conflicts before any quota check. Entries and their
samples are then applied in input order, so a later entry sees the earlier
entries of the same batch: a same-value restatement is a duplicate, a
differing value conflicts unless `overwrite` (then it replaces and counts as
written). The result is `{"written","duplicates","results"}` with one
`{"series_id","written","duplicates"}` per entry in input order; the totals
are the per-entry sums. A successful batch with `written > 0` increases
`stats()["writes"]` by exactly one; a pure-duplicate batch increases nothing.
Quotas are charged per tenant with the batch's net new series and distinct new
timestamps — duplicates and overwrites add no occupancy, and only dimensions
that actually increase are checked. Any rejection (structure, missing fields,
per-entry validation, future samples → `400`; conflict or quota → `409`)
leaves no series, sample or write-count change behind, on disk included, and
concurrent queries and quota reads only ever see the state before or after the
whole batch. Replaying the same batch re-judges duplicates and overwrites in
the same order.

**Snapshot export and replay.** `export_snapshot(tenant, metric, labels=None,
start_ms=None, end_ms=None, matchers=None)` (also `GET /v1/export` and the CLI
`export`) captures the raw samples of every matching series as a verifiable
document `{"version": 1, "snapshot_id": ..., "entries": [...]}`. The filters
and the closed `[start_ms, end_ms]` interval behave exactly as in `query`.
Each entry holds only `tenant`, `metric`, `labels` and `samples` (ascending by
timestamp); entries are ordered by `series_id` and registered series with no
sample in range are omitted. `snapshot_id` is the SHA-256 of the sorted,
compact JSON UTF-8 bytes of `{"version": 1, "entries": [...]}`. The export
reads one coherent snapshot under a single lock acquisition and never changes
write counters, quotas, alerts or query results, so exporting the same state
twice yields identical content.

`replay_snapshot(snapshot, now_ms=None, overwrite=False, dry_run=False)` (also
`POST /v1/replay` and the CLI `replay --snapshot '<json>'`) verifies the
document before storing anything: the version must be 1, `snapshot_id` must
match the entries digest, and every entry then goes through the `write_batch`
rules (labels, samples, future timestamps against `now_ms` when given,
conflicts, per-tenant quotas). Invalid input or a digest mismatch is a `400`,
a conflict or quota breach a `409`, and any failure leaves no in-memory or
on-disk change behind. The result is `{"written", "duplicates", "results",
"applied"}` with `results` in entry order. A dry run (`dry_run=true` /
`--dry-run`) performs all validation and counting but applies nothing and
reports `applied: false`; a real replay reports `applied: true` (`202` over
HTTP, `200` for a dry run). Replaying a snapshot onto the state it came from
is a pure duplicate replay (`written == 0`, the write counter does not move),
replaying onto a partial state fills in only the missing points, and a replay
after a restart re-judges exactly as an in-process one. Replay never mints new
series identities and does not alter labels, tenant isolation, query
aggregation, alert or SLO semantics. With access control enabled, export is a
`read` operation scoped to the requested tenant and replay is a `write`
operation checked per entry — any entry outside the caller's scope rejects the
whole replay with `403` — and both are audited like every other endpoint.

**Bucketing.** `query(..., step_ms=step, agg=agg)` assigns a sample with
timestamp `t` to bucket `b = t - (t % step)`, i.e. buckets are
left-closed/right-open (`[b, b+step)`) on epoch multiples. Every bucket from the
first non-empty bucket to the last non-empty bucket that also lies inside
`[start_ms, end_ms]` is emitted, and buckets with no sample are emitted as
`[b, null]`. Bucket value = `agg` over the samples in the bucket, where `agg` is
one of `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`. A series whose range contains no
sample is still listed with an empty `points` list. With `agg` and *no*
`step_ms` the whole `[start_ms, end_ms]` range is a single bucket. With neither,
raw samples are returned in `[timestamp, value]` order. `rollup(tenant, metric,
labels, window_ms, agg)` is `query` with `step_ms = window_ms` over the whole
stored range, with empty buckets dropped; output is ordered by `series_id`, so
it is deterministic.

**Label matchers.** In addition to exact `labels` / `label.k=v` filtering,
`query` accepts `matchers` (`matchers` on `GET /v1/query`, `--matchers` on the
CLI): a JSON array of objects containing exactly `key` (non-empty string),
`op` and `value` (string, may be empty). Ops are `=` / `!=` (exact whole-string
equality and negation) and `=~` / `!~` (Python `re` syntax matched against the
*whole* label value via full match, case-sensitive and Unicode-aware, and its
negation). Omitting the parameter, passing Python `None`, or sending `[]` adds
no condition; an explicit JSON `null` or empty text is rejected (HTTP/CLI).
Matchers combine with each other and with the exact label filters by logical
AND — including several matchers on the same key — apply to raw series labels
before bucketing or grouping (labels absent from `group_by` count too), and are
restricted to the requested `tenant` and `metric`; `tenant`, `metric` and
`series_id` are not implicit labels. A missing key never satisfies `=`/`=~` but
always satisfies `!=`/`!~`, so `=~ ""` selects only series where the key exists
with an empty value (grouping still separates a missing key from an empty
value). `api-.*` matches `api-a` but not `xapi-a`. Duplicate matchers never
duplicate series, matcher order is irrelevant, and contradictory matchers
yield an empty result. Invalid JSON, a non-array, non-object elements, missing
or extra fields, wrong types, an empty `key`, an unsupported `op` or an invalid
regex raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON error line on stderr for the
CLI); every matcher is validated even when no candidate series exists.

**Grouped query.** `query(..., agg=agg, group_by=[keys...])` aggregates *across*
series: matching series (same tenant/metric/label filters and `[start_ms,
end_ms]` range as above) are bucketed into groups by the values of the given
label keys, and the raw in-range samples of all series in a group are pooled
before `agg` is applied — samples from different series at the same timestamp
count individually. `group_by=[]` merges every matching series into one group.
Each result row carries only `labels` (the group keys actually present on the
group's series — a missing key and an empty-string value form different
groups) and `points`; rows are ordered lexicographically by their sorted label
pairs. Bucketing follows the same rules as the per-series query (epoch-aligned
left-closed buckets with `null` gaps, or a single point at the group's
earliest sample without `step_ms`). A group whose series have no sample in
range is still listed with empty `points`; no matching series at all yields an
empty `series` array. `group_by` must be a list of distinct non-empty strings
and requires `agg`; violations raise `ObsError` (`400` over HTTP, one JSON
error line on stderr for the CLI).

**Sliding-window query.** `query(..., start_ms=start, end_ms=end, step_ms=step,
agg=agg, window_ms=window)` switches to a separate mode the moment `window_ms`
is supplied (it is optional in every binding: `window` on `GET /v1/query`,
`--window-ms` on the CLI). In this mode `start_ms`, `end_ms`, `step_ms` and
`agg` are all required; `start_ms` and `end_ms` must be integer milliseconds,
`step_ms` and `window_ms` positive integer milliseconds, and `end_ms >=
start_ms` (bools, fractions and missing/unknown values are rejected). Evaluation
times are `t = start + k*step` for `k = 0, 1, ...`, keeping only times
`t <= end`; the output point timestamp is the evaluation time itself. The step
need not divide the window and windows are never aligned to fixed buckets.

Each evaluation aggregates the raw samples in the half-open interval
`(t - window_ms, t]`: the left edge is excluded (a sample exactly one window
length earlier does not count), the right edge included (a sample at `t`
does). `start_ms` only constrains the output grid — the first window at
`start` also reads history older than `start`; no window ever reads a sample
newer than its own evaluation time. The aggregation uses the same meanings as
bucketing (`sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count`), and a window containing no
sample emits `[t, null]` for *every* aggregation, including `count`.

Every matching registered series is returned on the full time grid even when
all of its windows are empty; no matching series yields an empty `series`
array. The Python per-series rows keep `series_id`; HTTP and CLI keep the
existing result shape. With `group_by`, all raw samples of the group's series
that fall in each window are pooled before aggregating (samples sharing a
timestamp across series count individually, `avg` divides by the total sample
count), a missing group key and an empty-string value stay distinct groups,
and each group keeps the full grid, fully null when no sample ever falls in a
window. Group filtering, ordering and validation follow the ordinary grouped
rules. The whole query reads one coherent snapshot, so concurrent writes or
retention sweeps can never mix old and new data; queries never alter samples,
counters or configuration, and the same history gives identical results after
reopening the store. Omitting `window_ms` preserves the previous query
behaviour exactly — `rollup`, write idempotency/overwrite, quotas, alerts and
SLOs are unaffected.

**Counter aggregates.** In sliding-window mode `agg` also accepts `increase`
and `rate` (query entries only — `rollup`, alert rules and SLOs still reject
them, and using them without `window_ms` fails the query). Each matching
series is treated as a counter: within `(t - window_ms, t]` the time-sorted
adjacent readings contribute their difference when non-decreasing, while a
drop is a counter reset contributing only the later reading; the first reading
contributes nothing. Only samples actually inside the window are used — no
boundary borrowing, interpolation or extrapolation by window length.
`increase` is the sum of those deltas, `rate` that sum divided by the seconds
between the window's first and last sample. A window with fewer than two
distinct sample timestamps emits `[t, null]`; unchanged readings emit `0`.
Grouped queries compute each series independently and sum the non-null
per-series results (never differencing across series); a group whose series
are all null at a time emits null there. Any matched sample that actually
falls into an output window and is negative or non-finite fails the whole
query (`ObsError`, HTTP `400`, CLI non-zero with a one-line JSON error);
samples outside every window or filtered out by labels/matchers are never
inspected, and parameters are validated even when no series matches.

**Retention.** `enforce_retention(tenant, cutoff_ms)` removes every sample of
that tenant with `timestamp_millis < cutoff_ms` and rewrites the affected point
files. `stats()` returns `{"series","points","writes","tenants"}`.

**Per-tenant quotas.** `set_quota(tenant, max_series, max_points)` sets the
tenant-wide limits; each limit is a non-negative integer or `null` (omitted
fields over HTTP also mean `null`, i.e. unlimited), and `0` forbids adding any.
`get_quota(tenant)` returns
`{"tenant","max_series","max_points","series","points"}` — the configured
limits and the current usage in one snapshot. Configuring a quota never creates
a series, and an unconfigured tenant is unlimited. Limits apply to all of a
tenant's metrics together: `series` is the number of registered series and
`points` the total number of *distinct timestamps* across those series, not
physical point-file lines. Label order, same-value replays, overwritten points
and a timestamp repeated inside one batch add no occupancy.

Every write path (`SeriesStore.write`/`write_batch`, `POST /v1/series` and
`/v1/series/batch`, the CLI `write`/`write-batch`) is
checked after the existing input validation and conflict rules, using the
batch's net increase: a batch is rejected (ObsError / HTTP `409` / CLI JSON
error with non-zero exit) when *either* dimension it increases would exceed its
limit, and the rejection leaves no new series, samples or write-count change.
Limits may be lowered below current usage; afterwards only the dimensions a
write actually increases are checked — an already-over-limit dimension blocks
nothing by itself, so pure duplicates and overwrites keep succeeding. Retention
frees the occupancy of deleted points, while empty series stay registered.
Overwrites rewrite the point file so one timestamp never occupies two lines; on
reopen, any duplicate timestamp lines (including those left by older builds)
collapse to the last value, so historical re-overwrites never double-count.

**Rule shape.** `{"id","tenant","metric","labels","comparator" ∈ {">",">=","<",
"<=","==","!="},"threshold","for_ms","window_ms","agg","severity" ∈ {"info",
"warning","critical"},"annotations"}`. `add_rule` validates every field and
raises `ObsError` for anything malformed (`id` is generated when omitted).

**Evaluation window.** Let `step = window_ms`, `t = now_ms` and
`bucket_start(t) = t - (t % step)`. The window is
`[bucket_start(t) - step, t]`, i.e. the current bucket plus the whole previous
bucket. The rule condition holds for a series when *every* non-empty bucket in
that window satisfies `comparator(value, threshold)` — one violating bucket
anywhere in the window stops the condition, and it keeps stopping it until that
bucket has left the window.

**`for_ms`.** Let `run_start` be the timestamp of the first bucket of the
current unbroken run of satisfying buckets (a violating bucket resets the run).
The rule fires only when the condition holds *and*
`bucket_start(now_ms) - run_start >= for_ms`. With `for_ms = 0`, one satisfied
bucket is enough; with `for_ms = window_ms`, the current and the previous bucket
must both be satisfied. Before the hold time is reached the alert is recorded
with `firing = false` and appears in none of the four output lists.

**Alert identity and dedup.** Alert identity is `(rule_id, series_id)`, distinct
from the alert id. The first time a condition holds an alert id
`alert-NNNNN` is minted for that identity and reused forever: re-evaluating an
unchanged condition returns the *same* `id` and increments `occurrences` (the
number of evaluations in which the condition held). `since_ms` is `run_start`,
not the evaluation time, so dedup does not depend on the wall clock.

**Resolution.** When the condition stops holding, the alert's state becomes
`resolved`, `firing` becomes `false`, `resolved_ms` is set once, and the alert is
reported in the `resolved` list of that evaluation. If the same condition holds
again later, the *same alert id* is reused and `occurrences` keeps counting.
Because the condition covers the whole window, a series that produced one bad
bucket stays unresolved until that bucket has left the window.

**Silence vs inhibition precedence.** A condition that holds and whose `for_ms`
is satisfied is first checked against active silences: a silence is active when
`starts_ms <= now_ms <= ends_ms`, the tenant matches and every silence label
matcher is present in the series labels. Inside an active silence the alert state
is `silenced` (it is *not* firing) and the silence id and reason are recorded.
Only if no silence matches is inhibition checked: an inhibition
`(source_severity, target_severity, same_labels)` marks a `target_severity` alert
as `inhibited` while an alert of at least `source_severity` is currently
`firing` in the same tenant with *exactly the same label set*. Silence therefore
wins over inhibition. A silenced or inhibited alert still counts its
`occurrences` and returns to `firing` as soon as the silence/inhibition no longer
applies. `list_alerts(state=None)` filters by `firing`, `silenced`, `inhibited`
or `resolved`.

**Notification routing.** `add_route({"tenant","target","labels"?,"severities"?,
"events"?,"repeat_ms"?,"id"?})` registers a notification route; `tenant` and
`target` are required non-empty strings, `labels` is an exact label subset the
alert's series must contain, `severities` (default: all severities) and
`events` (default: `["firing","resolved"]`, the only two allowed values) are
non-empty arrays when given, and `repeat_ms` is `null` or a non-negative
integer. Invalid shapes raise `ObsError` (HTTP `400`), a duplicate `id` is a
conflict (HTTP `409`), an unknown route is `404`; without an `id` the route is
named `route-NNNN`. Deleting a route keeps its historical notifications.

`evaluate(now_ms)` still returns only the four state lists, but every alert
transition also appends to the notification queue of each matching route
(tenant equal, route labels a subset of the series labels, alert severity in
`severities`): an alert that enters `firing` — the first time, or when
recovering from `silenced`/`inhibited` — produces one `firing` record; while
the same firing state continues a repeat is emitted only when `repeat_ms` is
set and that much time has passed since the route's last notification for the
alert; entering `resolved` produces exactly one `resolved` record. Pending
(`for_ms` not yet met), silenced and inhibited alerts never produce `firing`
records. Dedup is tracked per route, so routes notify independently. Each
record is `{"id": "notification-NNNNN","route_id","alert_id","tenant",
"target","event","created_ms","alert": <snapshot>,"acked": false}` and is
persisted across restarts together with the dedup state.
`list_notifications(tenant, route_id, alert_id, acked)` reads the queue
without consuming it; `ack_notification(id)` marks a record acknowledged,
returns the same record on a repeated ack and raises `ObsError` (HTTP `404`)
for an unknown id.

**SLO and error budget.** `set_slo(tenant, name, metric, labels,
good_comparator, threshold, target_ratio, window_ms)` defines a good-events
ratio SLO. `slo_status(name, now_ms, tenant=None)` counts every stored sample of
the matching series inside `[now_ms - window_ms, now_ms]`:

```
total          = number of samples in the window (nulls excluded)
good           = samples where compare(value, good_comparator, threshold)
bad            = total - good
ratio          = good / total                             (0.0 when total == 0)
error_budget   = max(0.0, 1 - (1 - ratio) / (1 - target_ratio))   (target_ratio < 1)
               = 1.0 if ratio >= 1.0 else 0.0              (target_ratio == 1)
burn_rate      = (bad / total) / (1 - target_ratio)        (0.0 when target_ratio >= 1 or total == 0)
met            = ratio >= target_ratio
```

`ratio` is the observed good ratio, `target_ratio ∈ (0,1]` the objective,
`burn_rate` how fast the budget is being spent relative to the allowed bad rate
(`1.0` means exactly on budget, `> 1.0` means burning too fast) and
`error_budget` the *fraction of the allowed error budget still unspent*:
`1.0` means untouched, `0.0` means exhausted or exceeded. For any `ratio` that
meets the target the two written forms of `error_budget` are identical, since
`1 - (1-ratio)/(1-target) = (ratio - target)/(1 - target)` and
`1 - ratio/target = (target - ratio)/target` are both non-negative only inside
their own regime; the first form is the one used, because it degrades sensibly
when the ratio beats the target (more budget left) instead of pinning to `0`.
With `total == 0` the ratio is `0.0`, so the budget counts as exhausted.

Examples: 9 good + 1 bad with `target_ratio = 0.9` gives `ratio = 0.9`,
`error_budget = 0.0`, `burn_rate = 0.1/0.1 = 1.0`, `met = true` (exactly on
budget). 98 good + 2 bad with `target_ratio = 0.95` gives `ratio = 0.98`,
`burn_rate = 0.02/0.05 = 0.4` and `error_budget = 1 - 0.02/0.05 = 0.6` (60% of
the budget still unspent). 90 good + 10 bad with `target_ratio = 0.99` gives
`ratio = 0.9`, `burn_rate = 10.0`, `error_budget = 0.0`, `met = false`.

**Determinism.** No module calls `time.time()` inside decision logic: `now_ms` is
passed into `evaluate`, `slo_status` and `write` (the HTTP layer uses the wall
clock only when a caller omits `now_ms` on `GET /v1/slos/status`, and
`/v1/slos/status` requires it in the CLI).

obsd/http_app.py    ThreadingHTTPServer + create_server

"""Tests for tenant retention policies and retention runs (store, CLI, HTTP)."""

import contextlib
import io
import json
import os
import shutil
import tempfile
import threading
import unittest
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

from obsd import AccessControl, AlertEngine, SeriesStore, create_server
from obsd.cli import main as cli_main
from obsd.tsdb import ObsError


class RetentionCase(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="obsd-retention-")
    def tearDown(self):
        shutil.rmtree(self.tmp, ignore_errors=True)
    def store(self, sub="data"):
        return SeriesStore(os.path.join(self.tmp, sub))


class TestRetentionPolicy(RetentionCase):
    def test_unconfigured_tenant_has_null_policy_and_real_usage(self):
        store = self.store()
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("acme"),
                         {"tenant": "acme", "retention_ms": None,
                          "series": 0, "points": 0})
        store.write("acme", "m", {}, [[1000, 1.0], [2000, 2.0]])
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("acme"),
                         {"tenant": "acme", "retention_ms": None,
                          "series": 1, "points": 2})

    def test_set_returns_normalised_policy_and_usage_without_series(self):
        store = self.store()
        out = store.set_retention("acme", 5000)
        self.assertEqual(out, {"tenant": "acme", "retention_ms": 5000,
                               "series": 0, "points": 0})
        self.assertEqual(store.stats()["series"], 0)
        self.assertTrue(os.path.exists(os.path.join(store.root, "retention.json")))
        store.write("acme", "m", {}, [[1, 1.0]])
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("acme")["retention_ms"], 5000)
        # Null means no cleanup and is a real configured policy.
        out = store.set_retention("acme", None)
        self.assertEqual(out["retention_ms"], None)
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("acme"),
                         {"tenant": "acme", "retention_ms": None,
                          "series": 1, "points": 1})

    def test_invalid_policy_raises_and_leaves_config_untouched(self):
        store = self.store()
        store.set_retention("acme", 1000)
        for bad_tenant in ("", None, 7):
            with self.assertRaises(ObsError, msg=repr(bad_tenant)):
                store.set_retention(bad_tenant, 1000)
        for bad_ms in (True, False, "1000", 1.5, -1, -0.5, []):
            with self.assertRaises(ObsError, msg=repr(bad_ms)):
                store.set_retention("acme", bad_ms)
        with self.assertRaises(ObsError):
            store.get_retention("")
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("acme")["retention_ms"], 1000)
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("globex")["retention_ms"], None)

    def test_policy_survives_reopen_and_legacy_dir_has_none(self):
        first = self.store("restart")
        first.set_retention("acme", 60_000)
        first.set_retention("globex", None)
        first.write("acme", "m", {}, [[1, 1.0]])
        second = self.store("restart")
        self.assertEqual(second.get_retention("acme"),
                         {"tenant": "acme", "retention_ms": 60_000,
                          "series": 1, "points": 1})
        self.assertIsNone(second.get_retention("globex")["retention_ms"])
        legacy = self.store("legacy")
        legacy.write("acme", "m", {}, [[1, 1.0]])
        self.assertFalse(os.path.exists(os.path.join(legacy.root, "retention.json")))
        self.assertIsNone(self.store("legacy").get_retention("acme")["retention_ms"])


class TestRetentionRun(RetentionCase):
    def seed(self, store, tenant="acme"):
        store.write(tenant, "m", {"k": "a"}, [[1000, 1.0], [2000, 2.0], [3000, 3.0]])
        store.write(tenant, "m", {"k": "b"}, [[500, 5.0], [2500, 6.0]])

    def test_cutoff_is_exclusive_and_boundary_point_is_kept(self):
        store = self.store()
        self.seed(store)
        store.set_retention("acme", 500)
        result = store.run_retention(2500, tenant="acme")
        # cutoff = 2500 - 500 = 2000; only timestamps < 2000 are dropped.
        self.assertEqual(result, {"dry_run": False, "tenants": [
            {"tenant": "acme", "cutoff_ms": 2000, "dropped": 3,
             "affected_series": 2, "remaining_points": 2,
             "compacted_series": 2}]})
        rows = store.query("acme", "m")
        self.assertEqual([row["points"] for row in rows],
                         [[[2500, 6.0]], [[2000, 2.0], [3000, 3.0]]])
        # The run is idempotent: a second identical run drops nothing.
        again = store.run_retention(2500, tenant="acme")
        self.assertEqual(again["tenants"][0]["dropped"], 0)
        self.assertEqual(again["tenants"][0]["remaining_points"], 2)

    def test_run_requires_integer_now_and_boolean_dry_run(self):
        store = self.store()
        store.set_retention("acme", 100)
        for bad_now in (None, True, 1.5, "1000"):
            with self.assertRaises(ObsError, msg=repr(bad_now)):
                store.run_retention(bad_now, tenant="acme")
        for bad_dry in (1, "true", None):
            with self.assertRaises(ObsError, msg=repr(bad_dry)):
                store.run_retention(1000, tenant="acme", dry_run=bad_dry)
        with self.assertRaises(ObsError):
            store.run_retention(1000, tenant="")
        self.assertEqual(store.stats()["writes"], 0)

    def test_null_policy_reports_null_cutoff_and_zero_deletions(self):
        store = self.store()
        self.seed(store)
        store.set_retention("acme", None)
        result = store.run_retention(10_000, tenant="acme")
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"], [
            {"tenant": "acme", "cutoff_ms": None, "dropped": 0,
             "affected_series": 0, "remaining_points": 5, "compacted_series": 0}])
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("acme")["points"], 5)
        # An explicit run for an unconfigured tenant behaves the same way.
        result = store.run_retention(10_000, tenant="globex")
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"][0]["cutoff_ms"], None)
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"][0]["dropped"], 0)

    def test_all_tenants_run_in_lexicographic_order(self):
        store = self.store()
        self.seed(store, "beta")
        self.seed(store, "alpha")
        self.seed(store, "unconfigured")
        store.set_retention("beta", 1000)
        store.set_retention("alpha", None)
        result = store.run_retention(3000)
        self.assertEqual([row["tenant"] for row in result["tenants"]],
                         ["alpha", "beta"])
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"][0]["cutoff_ms"], None)
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"][1]["cutoff_ms"], 2000)
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"][1]["dropped"], 3)
        # A tenant without a configured policy is not part of the sweep.
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("unconfigured")["points"], 5)

    def test_dry_run_changes_nothing_but_reports_everything(self):
        store = self.store()
        self.seed(store)
        store.set_retention("acme", 500)
        before_files = {name: open(os.path.join(store.points_dir, name)).read()
                        for name in os.listdir(store.points_dir)}
        result = store.run_retention(2500, tenant="acme", dry_run=True)

        # Memory, files, quota usage and the write counter are untouched.
        self.assertEqual(store.get_retention("acme")["points"], 5)
        self.assertEqual(store.stats()["writes"], 2)
        after_files = {name: open(os.path.join(store.points_dir, name)).read()
                       for name in os.listdir(store.points_dir)}
        self.assertEqual(before_files, after_files)

    def test_empty_series_stay_registered_and_free_quota_for_reuse(self):
        store = self.store()
        store.set_quota("acme", 2, 2)
        self.seed(store)
        store.set_retention("acme", 0)
        result = store.run_retention(10_000, tenant="acme")
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"][0]["dropped"], 5)
        self.assertEqual(result["tenants"][0]["remaining_points"], 0)
        # Both series are still registered with zero points.
        usage = store.get_quota("acme")
        self.assertEqual((usage["series"], usage["points"]), (2, 0))
        rows = store.query("acme", "m")
        self.assertEqual(len(rows), 2)
        self.assertEqual([row["points"] for row in rows], [[], []])
        # The freed occupancy is immediately available for new writes.
        self.assertEqual(store.write("acme", "m", {"k": "a"},
                                     [[20_000, 1.0], [21_000, 2.0]])["written"], 2)
